meta.title: Nothing New to Learn on the Neck
meta.summary: Every mode in this pathway is a CAGED window you already own with a degree or two moved — there is no new shape anywhere in six chapters.

spans.text: You already know the five CAGED windows of A major and the five of A minor. That's all ten, and every mode in this pathway is one of them with a degree moved — six of the seven need exactly one moved, and Locrian, the odd one out, needs two. There is no new shape anywhere in six chapters.
A window is anchored on the root, not the quality —
The Window Stays, the Third Moves
taught you that for major against minor, and it holds here too. A Dorian's E form covers the same frets, 4 to 8, that A minor's E form does.
Here's the E form of each, drawn as everything in the window rather than as a grip a hand would actually hold. The first card heads itself A minor, which is Aeolian under the name the app prints:

spans.text: Here's the honest part, and it matters more than the shapes themselves. The two scales differ by exactly one degree — every
— but "the same picture with one dot moved" is false as a caption for what you just saw. Both windows above hold seventeen dots. Equal counts. Different picture.
Positions below are written string, then fret — string 1 is the high e, string 6 the low E, the numbering the app uses everywhere. A Aeolian's
simply steps up one fret to
, which is off the top of the window entirely — so that copy drops out of the picture — while the

steps in from below instead. One dot fell off the top edge while a different one climbed in at the bottom, which is how the count comes out equal. So don't count dots to tell the two apart: a window is a fixed span of frets, and how many dots land inside it depends on where its edges happen to fall. In this window it comes to seventeen either way. In the D form, the next window up the neck at frets 6 to 10, it comes to eighteen for Aeolian and seventeen for Dorian.
